courses.name: General Physics II
weekTopics: A transformer transfers energy between two circuits by mutual induction: a primary winding of N1 turns and a secondary of N2 turns on a laminated soft-iron core, the core increasing the magnetic flux and carrying it from one coil to the other. It works only on AC, because the secondary emf is -N2 dPhi/dt and a steady DC current gives a steady core flux and hence zero induced emf.

The transformer equation V2/V1 = N2/N1 (voltages rms, in volts; turns are pure numbers) follows because the same changing core flux threads every turn of both windings, so V1 = -N1 dPhi/dt and V2 = -N2 dPhi/dt give V1/N1 = V2/N2. N2 > N1 is step-up, N2 < N1 is step-down, N2 = N1 is an isolation transformer; the frequency of the output always equals that of the source.

In an ideal transformer there are no winding or core losses, so P1 = P2, i.e. V1 I1 = V2 I2 and I1/I2 = N2/N1 = V2/V1: the current ratio is the inverse of the voltage ratio, so voltage is gained only at the cost of current and no energy is created. Real efficiency is eta = P_out/P_in x 100%, typically 90-99%.

A transformer also transforms resistance: a load R on the secondary appears to the source as R_apparent = (N1/N2)^2 R, with the SQUARE of the turns ratio. Choosing the turns ratio so that this equals the source's own internal resistance is impedance matching, which gives maximum power transfer from source to load.

Real losses and their cures: copper loss (I^2 R heating in the windings, reduced by thicker low-resistance conductors, and load-dependent); eddy-current loss (currents induced in the core, reduced by laminating it into thin insulated sheets); hysteresis loss (energy per cycle to reverse the core's magnetisation, reduced by a soft magnetic material); plus flux leakage and mechanical/humming loss. Eddy and hysteresis are core losses and continue at no load.

Power is transmitted at high voltage because for a fixed delivered power P the line current is I = P/V, so the line waste is P_loss = I^2 R_line = P^2 R_line / V^2 and falls as the inverse square of the transmission voltage; AC beats DC for distribution precisely because transformers can step the voltage up for the line and back down for homes and businesses.

courses.name: Elementary Mathematics II (Calculus)
weekTopics: Net change / accumulation: if a quantity changes at rate r(t) then the total change over [a,b] is ∫ₐᵇ r(t) dt = f(b) − f(a); the units of the integral are (units of r)×(units of t), which is what identifies the answer as litres, joules, newtons, naira or kilograms. The average value of the rate is (1/(b−a))∫ₐᵇ r dt, not r at the midpoint.

Kinematics: antidifferentiate a(t) to get v(t) and v(t) to get s(t), each step fixed by an initial condition (v(0), s(0)). Displacement over [a,b] is ∫ₐᵇ v dt; total distance is ∫ₐᵇ |v| dt, obtained by splitting the interval at the zeros of v and adding magnitudes.

Work by a variable force: W = ∫ₐᵇ F(x) dx, valid because the force is effectively constant on a slice of width dx. For a spring obeying Hooke's law F = kx (k from a measured force and extension), W = ½k(b² − a²); F × d is only correct for a constant force.

Fluid force on a vertically submerged plate: pressure at depth h is ρgh, so the strip at depth h of width w(h) carries force ρg·h·w(h)dh and F = ρg∫ₐᵇ h·w(h) dh, with h measured downwards from the free surface (water: ρg = 9800 N/m³). Equivalent check: F = ρg·h̄·A with h̄ the centroid depth.

Marginal analysis: C(q) = ∫₀^q MC dq + C(0) where C(0) is fixed cost, and the extra cost from q₁ to q₂ is ∫_{q₁}^{q₂} MC dq with no fixed cost involved; likewise R(q) = ∫₀^q MR dq. Profit change is ∫(MR − MC) dq and is maximised where MR = MC, an output the fixed cost cannot move.

Consumer and producer surplus: solve D(q) = S(q) for the equilibrium (q₀, p₀), then CS = ∫₀^{q₀}[D(q) − p₀]dq (area between the demand curve and the price line) and PS = ∫₀^{q₀}[p₀ − S(q)]dq (area between the price line and the supply curve); their sum is the total surplus used to judge market efficiency.

Environmental science: the cumulative amount of pollutant discharged over [0,T] is ∫₀^T r(t) dt, with ∫₀^T Ae^{kt} dt = (A/k)(e^{kT} − 1); population change is P(T) = P₀ + ∫₀^T r(t) dt, and constant relative growth P′ = kP gives P = P₀e^{kt}.

courses.name: Introduction to Problem Solving
weekTopics: The software testing life cycle: six phases in sequential order — requirement analysis, test planning, test case development, test environment setup, test execution, test cycle closure — each with an entry point where it begins and an exit point reached only when all the objectives of that phase have been achieved.

What each STLC phase owns: requirement analysis decides what is to be tested (document review, stakeholder interviews, issue identification); test planning fixes strategy, cost, duration and roles; test case development writes and reviews cases specifying inputs, process and expected outputs; test environment setup specifies software and hardware; test execution runs, retests and reports; test cycle closure confirms objectives met, writes the summary report and collects feedback.

Debugging as the process of identifying and resolving errors or bugs in a software system, distinct from testing, which only finds out whether the given output matches the expected output. Its methods are code inspection, monitoring, logging, unit, integration and system testing, and debugging tools — debuggers (Radare2, WinDbg, Valgrind), trace tools and profilers.

Functional testing methods, which check that the program performs as expected: unit testing on execution paths within functions, integration testing of how parts work together (top-down tests higher-level modules first, bottom-up tests lower-level modules first), system testing of the integrated whole against technical and functional requirements, and acceptance testing against expected requirements.

Non-functional testing methods, which check how well the software behaves rather than what it does: usability testing by observing users, performance testing for network, database and client-side delays under different load conditions, security testing for data security, availability, confidentiality and integrity, and compatibility testing across browsers, platforms and operating systems.

Black box, white box and grey box testing, separated purely by how much of the internal structure the tester knows: black box (unknown; integration, system, acceptance), white box (known, inputs chosen to exercise paths through the code, programming know-how essential; unit, integration, system), grey box (partially known, internals used to design the cases but tests run at the user level; primarily integration).

Designing test data in practice: equivalence partitioning takes one representative from each class the program should treat identically, boundary value analysis adds the values just below, at and just above each edge, and a debugger's breakpoint, step and variable watch locate where program state first becomes wrong so the defect class can be named.

courses.name: General Physics Practical II
weekTopics: Stress σ = F/A in N/m² (Pa), strain ε = Δℓ/ℓ (dimensionless), and Hooke's law σ = Eε, valid only below the proportional limit.
Young modulus E = stress/strain = Fℓ/(AΔℓ), unit N/m² = Pa; a measure of stiffness, about 70 GPa for aluminium and 120 GPa for copper. (The deck misprints the unit as N/m.)
Central depression of a beam of length ℓ loaded with mass m at its midpoint: Y = mgℓ³/(48EI), the beam treated as two opposite cantilevers, g = 9.8 m/s².
Rectangular cross-section second moment I = bd³/12 (b = breadth, d = thickness), giving the linear working equation Y = mgℓ³/(4Ebd³).
Graph of depression Y (m) against load m (kg): a straight line through the origin of gradient s = gℓ³/(4Ebd³) in m/kg, hence E = gℓ³/(4bd³s).

Apparatus (dial gauge, beams of different materials, set of masses, 2 mounts), the 50 g to 500 g loading procedure, and the dominant error: d is cubed, so a 5% error in thickness gives about 15% error in E.

checks.topic: Applications of integration treated conceptually: why integrating a rate over an interval gives the total change (the net change theorem) and how units confirm it, why acceleration alone cannot determine velocity without an initial condition, the difference between displacement ∫v dt and distance ∫|v| dt and why the sign of v forces a split, why a varying force gives W = ∫F dx rather than F×d and why a vertical submerged plate must be cut into horizontal strips of pressure ρgh, what the constant of integration in C(q) = ∫MC dq + K actually is, what consumer surplus measures as an area, and why an average value is the total divided by the interval length rather than the midpoint value.

questions.q: A tank is being filled at a rate r(t) litres per minute, t in minutes. The quantity ∫₃⁷ r(t) dt represents:
options: the number of litres added to the tank between t = 3 and t = 7
the rate at which the tank is filling at t = 7, in litres per minute
the average filling rate over those four minutes, in litres per minute
the increase in the filling rate between t = 3 and t = 7, in litres per minute
questions.concept: Net change theorem: integrating a rate over an interval gives the total accumulated, and the units multiply out
questions.why: r dt has units (litres/min)(min) = litres, and ∫₃⁷ r dt = V(7) − V(3), the volume added over the interval; the rate at an instant, the average rate and the change in the rate are all different quantities.

questions.q: Knowing the acceleration a(t) of a body for every t is still not enough to determine its velocity v(t) because:
options: acceleration can be negative, and a negative integrand makes the integral ambiguous
integrating acceleration produces a quantity with units of distance, so a term with units of velocity must be added to it
a definite integral cannot be evaluated until both of its limits have been specified
antidifferentiation fixes v only up to an additive constant, and that constant is the velocity at the chosen starting instant — the same acceleration history is consistent with any initial speed
questions.concept: The constant of integration in a → v → s, fixed by an initial condition
questions.why: Two bodies pushed identically but launched at different speeds have the same a(t) and different v(t); the antiderivative is determined only up to +C, and v(0) is what pins C down. (Integrating m/s² over s gives m/s, not distance.)

questions.q: A particle moves along a line with velocity v(t) that changes sign somewhere inside [a,b]. Then:
options: ∫ₐᵇ v dt is the total distance travelled, and ∫ₐᵇ |v| dt is the displacement
∫ₐᵇ v dt is the displacement; the total distance is ∫ₐᵇ |v| dt, evaluated by splitting the interval at the zeros of v
the two are equal, since displacement and distance always agree over a closed interval
∫ₐᵇ v dt is the displacement, and the total distance is |∫ₐᵇ v dt|
questions.concept: Signed versus unsigned accumulation: displacement ∫v dt against distance ∫|v| dt
questions.why: A negative v contributes negatively, so ∫v dt lets backward motion cancel forward motion — exactly what displacement is; distance needs |v|, and the zeros of v are where the integrand changes formula. Taking the modulus after integrating cancels first and so still loses the backtracking.

questions.q: The work done by a force F(x) as an object moves from x = a to x = b is ∫ₐᵇ F(x) dx rather than F × (b − a) because:
options: force and displacement are vectors, and a product of vectors must be written as an integral
work is the area under the force–time graph, so time has to be integrated out

on a sub-interval short enough that F is essentially constant the work is F(x)Δx; adding those contributions and letting Δx → 0 is exactly the integral, and F × (b − a) is correct only when F does not vary
the integration is what converts newton-metres into joules
questions.concept: Slice-and-sum: a varying quantity is constant on a small enough slice, and the sum of the slices is the integral
questions.why: Work is force times displacement only while the force is constant, so the interval is cut into pieces on which F barely changes, the elementary works F(x)Δx are added, and the limit is ∫ₐᵇ F dx; the graph involved is force against position, not time.

questions.q: A plate is submerged vertically in a liquid of weight density ρg. The force on one face is found by cutting the plate into **horizontal** strips because:
options: the pressure ρgh depends only on the depth, so it is constant along a horizontal strip but different for every strip; the force on one strip is (ρgh)·w(h)dh and these must be added
the width of the plate varies with depth while the pressure does not
pressure acts vertically downwards, so vertical strips would feel no force at all
the force equals the weight of the column of liquid standing directly above the plate, and that column must be integrated over its height
questions.concept: Fluid pressure depends only on depth, so the strip must be a line of constant depth
questions.why: Every point of a horizontal strip is at the same depth h and so at the same pressure ρgh; that makes force = pressure × area usable on the strip, giving dF = ρg·h·w(h)dh, and F = ρg∫h·w(h)dh. A vertical strip would span many depths and so many pressures.

questions.q: If the marginal cost C′(q) = MC(q) is known, then C(q) = ∫MC(q) dq + K, where K is:
options: the marginal cost of the first unit produced
zero, since producing nothing costs nothing
the average cost per unit at the break-even output
the fixed cost C(0) — the cost already incurred at zero output, which no amount of marginal information can supply
questions.concept: The constant of integration in total cost is the fixed cost; marginal data determines only changes
questions.why: Setting q = 0 in C(q) = ∫₀^q MC dq + K gives K = C(0). Rent and plant costs are paid at zero output, so C(0) ≠ 0 in general, and no derivative can detect a constant.

questions.q: At the equilibrium price p₀ and quantity q₀, the consumer surplus CS = ∫₀^{q₀}[D(q) − p₀] dq measures:
options: the total amount the consumers actually pay for the q₀ units
the total of the amounts consumers would have been willing to pay over and above what they did pay, added up across all q₀ units
the revenue producers receive in excess of what it cost them to produce the q₀ units
the amount the buyer of the very last unit would have paid, minus the price of that unit
questions.concept: Consumer surplus as the area between the demand curve and the price line
questions.why: D(q) is what the buyer of the q-th unit would have paid; D(q) − p₀ is that buyer's gain, and integrating adds the gains of all q₀ buyers. What consumers actually pay is p₀q₀; the producers' analogue is producer surplus; and the last unit's gain is a single value of the integrand, not the integral.

questions.q: A pollutant enters a lake at rate r(t) = 20 + 3t² kg/month. The average discharge rate over the first six months is (1/6)∫₀⁶ r(t) dt, and this is **not** equal to r(3) because:
options: the mean value theorem for integrals applies only to increasing functions
an average rate is obtained by dividing the total discharged by the total, not by the elapsed time

the average value is the height of the rectangle having the same area as the region under r; that height coincides with the midpoint value only when r is linear (or symmetric about the midpoint), and this r is quadratic
r(3) is the median rate over the interval, and the median of a positive function always exceeds its mean
questions.concept: Average value of a function = (1/(b−a))∫ₐᵇ f, i.e. the equal-area rectangle height
questions.why: Here the total is 336 kg so the average is 56 kg/month, while r(3) = 47: the curve rises faster than linearly, so the later months contribute more area than the midpoint rectangle allows. Averaging divides by the interval length, which is what makes the units come out as kg/month.

questions.q: State the theorem that makes "integrate the rate to get the total" true, and explain using units why ∫₀^{10} r(t) dt is a number of kilograms when r is measured in kilograms per day. Say what the same integral would mean if r were instead a concentration in mg/L.
questions.concept: The net change theorem and dimensional analysis of an integral
questions.why: The net change theorem (a form of the Fundamental Theorem): if Q is differentiable with Q′ = r, then ∫ₐᵇ r(t)dt = Q(b) − Q(a), so integrating the rate of change recovers the total change. Dimensionally, r dt carries (kg/day)(day) = kg, and the integral is a limit of sums of such terms, so it is a mass in kg — 10 days of discharge. If r were a concentration in mg/L, r dt would carry (mg/L)(day) = mg·day/L, which is an exposure or area-under-the-curve (as in pharmacokinetics), not a mass: to get a mass you must integrate a rate of input, not a concentration.

questions.q: A particle's velocity is positive on part of [0,4] and negative on the rest. Explain the difference between its displacement and the distance it travels, what you must do to the integral to get the distance, and why the sign of v is what forces that step.
questions.concept: Displacement versus total distance, and splitting at the zeros of the velocity
questions.why: Displacement is the net change in position, s(4) − s(0) = ∫₀⁴ v dt; distance is how far the particle actually moves, ∫₀⁴|v|dt. Where v < 0 the integrand is negative and the integral subtracts that motion, which is right for displacement (the particle really has come back) and wrong for distance. To get the distance, find the zeros of v inside [0,4], integrate v over each sub-interval separately, take the absolute value of each result and add them. The two agree only when v does not change sign; otherwise distance > |displacement|.

questions.q: Work done by a variable force and fluid force on a vertical plate are set up by the same manoeuvre. Explain what the thin slice is in each case and what quantity is treated as constant on it, and explain why (pressure at the top edge) × (area of the plate) is not the fluid force.
questions.concept: One slicing principle behind W = ∫F dx and F = ρg∫h·w(h)dh
questions.why: In both, the region is cut into pieces small enough that the varying quantity is effectively constant on each piece, the elementary contribution is written, and the pieces are integrated. For work the slice is a displacement dx over which F(x) is taken as constant, giving dW = F(x)dx. For fluid force the slice is a horizontal strip of thickness dh at depth h, over which the pressure ρgh is constant (pressure depends only on depth), giving dF = ρg·h·w(h)dh. Using the pressure at the top edge assumes the whole plate feels the smallest pressure it experiences, so it underestimates the force; the bottom-edge pressure overestimates it. The only single pressure that works is the one at the centroid depth, F = ρg·h̄·A.

questions.q: Explain why marginal cost alone determines total cost only up to a constant, say exactly what that constant is, and explain why the extra cost of raising output from q = 2 to q = 5 can still be computed without knowing it.
questions.concept: Fixed cost as the constant of integration; definite integrals of MC give changes only
questions.why: MC is the derivative of C, and any two functions differing by a constant have the same derivative, so antidifferentiating MC gives C only up to +K. Putting q = 0 identifies K = C(0), the fixed cost — rent, plant, licences — which is paid before any unit is made and which no marginal information can reveal. The extra cost of moving from q = 2 to q = 5 is C(5) − C(2) = ∫₂⁵ MC dq, and the K in C(5) and C(2) cancels in the subtraction; the fixed cost is already spent and is not incurred again. Adding it to that answer is a standard error.
